chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon them), that he said:

Regarding two men, for each of them there was food with his companion, and each of them did not know how much was for him with his companion. So each one of them said to his companion, 'For you is what is with you, and for me is what is with me.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'There is no problem with that if they are both pleased and their souls are content.'

key_terms.تراضيا: They mutually agreed / were pleased with each other
key_terms.صاحب: Companion / owner of the other's property

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on exchanging goods when the exact quantities are unknown but both parties agree?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Kafi, the Imam (peace be upon him) validates a mutual exchange of unknown quantities of food, emphasizing that validity rests on *tarāḍā* (mutual consent) and *ṭayyib al-nafs* (contentment of the soul) rather than precise measurement. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential principle that in transactions involving uncertainty (*gharar*), the parties' voluntary agreement suffices to remove the defect, provided there is no explicit prohibition. It highlights the flexibility in Islamic commercial law to facilitate ease (*taysīr*) among believers when exact accounting is impractical.
